# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-2 (Extended v17)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; 1809 (Pope's arrest); 1811 (Bishop's synod attendance); 1813 onward (Napoleon's decline); 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, early October—around sunset); present day (spring transitioning to late August/early September, England); future wedding (following spring); **1795 (Jean Valjean's theft and trial at age approximately 25-26)**
- Primary locations: England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Dunstead/Kelford harbor towns, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere); Secondary locations: San Francisco, New York, Eastern Prussia, Germany, Hamburgh; French locations (D——, Manosque, Sisteron, Hautes-Alpes, Paris, Italy, Durance, Château-Arnoux, Senez, Briançon, Aix, Draguignan, Embrun, Chastelar, Arche, Barcelonette, Jauziers, Tuiles, Joug-de-l'Aigle, Ubaye, Ubayette, Ollioules, Nice, Piédmont, Couloubrieux, Cannes, Rue Cassette, Elmhaven, Staveford, Grenoble, Bras d'Asse, Escoublon, Grasse, Franche-Comté, **Pontarlier, Lods, Châtillon, Audincourt, Beure, Faverolles, Brie, Tottlingen, Toulon**); **Majore (Marseilles); Danube sources**
- **October 1815, early month, D——: About one hour before sunset, a man entered town on foot. Atmosphere: rain threatening since morning but holding off; frost silvered hedges overnight; chalked sun on forge wall; gulls quarreling over fish heads; salt and tar smell on wind; smoke lying flat; bell for vespers ringing thinly; baker's boy late, line at oven long; thaw left road rutted and puddled. At eight o'clock evening: Bishop at writing, Madame Magloire preparing supper, household about to dine. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage; children chased hoop down lane shrieking; cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Light went early as it did that time of year.**

## Main Characters and Relationships

**M. Charles Myriel / Monseigneur Bienvenu / Monseigneur Welcome (Bishop)**
- French aristocrat; family ruined by Revolution; emigrated to Italy; wife died in Italy
- Became priest, then Bishop of D——; encountered Napoleon circa coronation epoch
- Redistributes entire 15,000 franc yearly State salary across 23 charitable categories; retains 1,500 francs yearly for personal sustenance
- Philosophy: society culpable for poverty and ignorance; universe appears as immense malady with permanent fever; strives to dress wounds and relieve suffering
- Attended condemned murderer's execution; upon knife falling, told sufferer God raises the slain, resulting in sufferer's radiance. Upon return, entered deep moral crisis: phantom of social justice tormented him; ruminated on scaffold as monstrous instrument.
- Daily life: Sleeps little; morning meditation one hour; says mass; breaks fast on rye bread dipped in milk; at eight o'clock evening, writes on little squares of paper; at half-past eight sups with sister extraordinarily frugal repast; after supper converses half hour then retires to write on loose sheets and margins
- Furniture sparse and austere: six silver knives, forks, and soup-ladle; two large candlesticks of massive silver; iron hospital bed with green serge canopy; bookcase cupboard with glass doors
- Garden: four alleys in cross-form radiating from tank with circumferential walk. Three plots for vegetables; fourth planted by Bishop with flowers and few fruit-trees
- House has no locked doors day or night; philosophy written on Bible margin: "This is the shade of difference: the door of the physician should never be shut, the door of the priest should always be open." When asked about risk, cited Scripture: "Nisi Dominus custodierit domum, in vanum vigilant qui custodiunt eam," Unless the Lord guard the house, in vain do they watch who guard it.
- **Bandit incident: After destruction of Gaspard Bès's band in Ollioules gorges, lieutenant Cravatte took refuge in mountains near Barcelonette. Bishop arrived at Chastelar. Mayor urged him to retrace steps; Bishop replied: "What would they say to bishop who was afraid?" Traveled alone fortnight preaching, administering sacrament, teaching. Upon return, large chest deposited by two unknown horsemen containing pontifical vestments stolen from Notre Dame d'Embrun treasury. Paper read: "From Cravatte to Monseigneur Bienvenu."**
- **1809: Summoned by Napoleon to synod of bishops at Paris (Pope arrested July 5-6)**
- **1811 (June 15): Attended synod at Notre-Dame under Cardinal Fesch. Remarked on luxuries: "They must be a great trouble. I would not have all those superfluities, crying: 'There are people who are hungry! There are people who are cold!'"**
- **Political views: Beginning 1813, gave adherence to all hostile manifestations against Napoleon. Refused to see him as he passed through on return from Elba. Acknowledged character flaw: Had his hour of party spirit, bitterness, cloud. Was Royalist.**
- **1815: Reached seventy-fifth birthday; did not appear more than sixty. Rather plump; took long strolls on foot; step firm; form slightly bent.**
- Character: Does not attempt to impart prophetic greatness; humble soul loved, and that was all. Inclined towards all that groans and all that expiates. Gazed upon God without seeking to comprehend. Considered magnificent conjunctions of atoms forming and dissolving incessantly, hence life and death. Divided leisure between gardening daytime and contemplation night.
- Besides sister Baptistine, had two brothers: one a general, other a prefect. Was harsh toward general for pursuing Emperor at Cannes disembarkation. More affectionate correspondence with ex-prefect brother living in retirement at Paris on Rue Cassette.
- **Current evening (October 1815): When Valjean at supper confesses his status, Bishop responds with warmth and dignity. Explains fruitières of Pontarlier to Valjean—divided into big barns belonging to rich (40-50 cows, 7,000-8,000 cheeses summer) and associated fruitières belonging to poor (peasants hold cows in common, share proceeds). Grurin (cheese-maker) receives milk three times daily, marks quantity on double tally. Work begins end of April; cheese-makers drive cows to mountains mid-June. After supper, Mother Gerbaud visits with child; Bishop kisses child on brow and borrows fifteen sous from Baptistine to give to Gerbaud. Tells Valjean: "You must be in great need of your bed." Says grace. Instructs Madame Magloire to clear table promptly. Later sends Madame Magloire with goat skin from Black Forest (in Baptistine's room) to Valjean's bed for warmth—skin old, hair falling out, purchased in Germany at Tottlingen near sources of Danube, along with little ivory-handled knife Baptistine uses at table. Nights are frigid. Knelt before curtain of alcove concealing altar, said brief prayer, then walked in garden meditating on grand and mysterious things God shows at night.**
- **After Valjean's meal: Made strange abrupt movement—folded arms, bent savage gaze upon guest, exclaimed in hoarse voice. Text does not specify words but indicates moment of intensity or warning; unclear if Bishop intended to convey warning or menace or obeyed obscure instinctive impulse.**

**Mademoiselle Baptistine** (Bishop's sister)
- Long, pale, thin, gentle creature; embodiment of respectability; acquired beauty of goodness
- Yearly income 500 francs for personal wants; subsists on shared 1,500 francs with bishop and servant
- Witnessed Bishop's deep moral crisis; shares confidence in his openness
- **Current evening: Perfectly peaceable and natural; takes seat at Bishop's left at supper table. Lends fifteen sous for Mother Gerbaud. Possesses goat skin from Black Forest and little ivory-handled knife.**

**Madame Magloire** (Bishop's servant)
- Only servant in household; subsists on shared 1,500 francs yearly
- Eventually accustomed herself to Bishop's openness
- **Current evening: Heard warnings about prowler of evil appearance—dangerous mendicant in town. Revealed that Labarre had not been willing to receive him. Vagabond had been seen arriving via boulevard Gassendi, roaming streets in gloaming. Proposed Bishop permit locksmith Paulin Musebois to replace ancient locks for this night. At supper, places three sets of forks and spoons; when Bishop has guest, usual usage of house to lay out all six sets of silver on tablecloth—innocent ostentation. After supper, cleared table very promptly to allow Valjean to sleep. Later carried goat skin from Black Forest to Valjean's bed.**

**Jean Valjean**
- **Born in poor peasant family of Brie; did not learn to read in childhood. Became tree-pruner at Faverolles upon reaching man's estate. Mother named Jeanne Mathieu; father called Jean Valjean or Vlajean, probably sobriquet and contraction of "voilà Jean" (here's Jean). Lost father and mother at very early age. Mother died of milk fever not properly attended to. Father, also tree-pruner, killed by fall from tree. Sister older than himself—widow with seven children, boys and girls—brought him up. So long as she had husband, lodged and fed young brother.**
- **At approximately 25-26 years, took father's place and supported sister who brought him up. This done simply as duty and churlishly on his part. Youth spent in rude and ill-paid toil. Had never known "kind woman friend" in native parts; had not had time to fall in love.**
- **Appearance upon arrival at D——, October 1815: Medium stature, thickset and robust, approximately 46 years old. Cap with drooping leather visor; face burned and tanned by sun and wind, dripping with perspiration; coarse yellow linen shirt fastened at neck by small silver anchor; hairy breast; cravat twisted into string; blue drilling trousers worn and threadbare, white on one knee, torn on other; old gray tattered blouse, patched on elbow with bit of green cloth sewn on with twine; soldier knapsack tightly packed, perfectly new, on back; enormous knotty stick in hand; iron-shod shoes on stockingless feet; shaved head and long beard.**
- **Disposition: Thoughtful but not gloomy; constituted peculiarity of affectionate natures. Something decidedly sluggish and insignificant about appearance.**
- **Early life hardships: Sister Jeanne often took best part of his repast—bit of meat, slice of bacon, heart of cabbage—to give to her children. As he ate with head bent over table, long hair falling about bowl and concealing eyes, had air of perceiving nothing and allowing it. At Faverolles, farmer's wife Marie-Claude lived on other side of lane. Valjean children, habitually famished, sometimes borrowed pint of milk in mother's name, drank behind hedge or alley corner, snatching jug so hastily little girls spilled it. Jean paid Marie-Claude gruffly and grumblingly behind mother's back; children not punished.**
- **During pruning season earned eighteen sous a day; hired out as hay-maker, laborer, neat-herd on farm, drudge. Did whatever he could. Sister worked but had seven little children. Sad group enveloped in misery, gradually annihilated. Very hard winter came. Jean had no work. Family had no bread. Literally no bread. Seven children.**
- **1795: Theft and trial—One Sunday evening, Maubert Isabeau, baker on Church Square at Faverolles, was preparing for bed when heard violent blow on grated shop front. Arm passed through hole made by fist, seized loaf of bread, carried it off. Isabeau ran out in haste; robber fled at full speed. Isabeau ran after and stopped him. Thief flung away loaf but arm still bleeding. It was Jean Valjean. Taken before tribunals of time for theft and breaking and entering inhabited house at night. Had gun which he used better than any one else in world; bit of poacher, which injured his case. Legitimate prejudice against poachers—they smack too strongly of brigand.**
- **Court found Valjean guilty. Code was explicit. Condemned to five years in galleys. Set out for Toulon on cart with chain on neck after 27-day journey. At Toulon clothed in red cassock. All that had constituted his life, even to his name, was effaced; he was no longer Jean Valjean; he was number 24,601.**
- **During imprisonment, fellow convicts and their fates became unknown to him; after one day's discussion about them, the connection closed. He heard nothing more forever; nothing from sister or children ever reached him again; never beheld, never met them again.**
- **In galleys: Initially believed he was not innocent man unjustly punished. Admitted theft was extreme and blameworthy act. Recognized loaf probably would not have been refused if asked; better to wait for compassion or work. Acknowledged rare to die literally of hunger; man constituted to suffer long and much morally and physically without dying; therefore necessary to have patience. Reflected it would have been better for seven children.**
- **Meditation upon injustice: During imprisonment, questioned whether he alone was at fault. Reflected society must care for laborers without work. Once fault committed and confessed, recognized chastisement ferocious and disproportioned. Recognized abuse of law in penalty exceeded culprit's fault; excess of weights on one scale of expiation. Over-weight of penalty equivalent to annihilation of crime, reversing situation, replacing fault of delinquent with fault of repression, converting guilty man into victim and debtor into creditor, ranging law on side of man who violated it. Penalty, complicated by successive aggravations for four escape attempts, became outrage perpetrated by stronger upon feebler; crime of society against individual, crime being committed afresh every day, crime lasting nineteen years.**
- **Questioned whether human society could force members to suffer equally for its own unreasonable lack of foresight and pitiless foresight; to seize poor man forever between defect and excess, default of work and excess of punishment. Declared to himself no equilibrium between harm caused and harm being done to him. Concluded punishment was not unjust but most assuredly iniquitous.**
- **Character transformation during imprisonment: Human society had done him nothing but harm; never seen except angry face called Justice shown to those struck. Men only touched him to bruise him. Every contact had been blow. Never since infancy, since days of mother and sister, encountered friendly word and kindly glance. From suffering to suffering, gradually arrived at conviction that life is war; in this war he was conquered. Had no other weapon than hate. Resolved to whet it in galleys and bear it away when departed.**
- **Education: At Toulon, school for convicts kept by Ignorantin friars where branches taught to those with mind for it. Valjean went to school at age 40, learned to read, write, cipher. Felt fortifying intelligence fortified his hate. Education and enlightenment can serve to eke out evil. Sentence extended: five years initial plus fourteen years for four escape attempts equals nineteen years total.**
- **Upon arrival at D——, October 1815: Walked from south (possibly seashore) on foot, same route Napoleon took from Cannes to Paris seven months previously. Appeared very fatigued after walking all day; drank from fountains. Turned left at corner of Rue Poichevert, proceeded toward town-hall; entered and left quarter hour later; pulled off cap and humbly saluted gendarme seated outside. Proceeded to Cross of Colbas inn; warmed himself before kitchen fire with back turned.**
- **Wandered streets forgetful of fatigue while sad. Felt pangs of hunger sharply as night drew near. Glanced through window of public house, saw men drinking, landlord warming himself, iron pot suspended from crane bubbling over flame. Approached, seated himself near hearth, stretched out exhausted feet to fire; fine odor emitted by pot. Face beneath cap assumed vague appearance of comfort mingled with poignant aspect.**
- **Fishmonger on road between Bras d'Asse and Escoublon had encountered him that morning; Valjean requested ride on crupper; fishmonger declined by redoubling gait. Fishmonger had been member of group surrounding Labarre at Cross of Colbas, related disagreeable encounter. From public house, fishmonger made imperceptible sign to tavern-keeper; they exchanged few words in low tone.**
- **Later: Entered little street with gardens enclosed only by hedges. Caught sight of small single-story house with lighted window. Peered through pane; within was large whitewashed room with bed draped in printed cotton stuff, cradle in corner, few wooden chairs, double-barrelled gun on wall. Table spread in centre; copper lamp illuminated coarse white linen tablecloth, pewter jug shining like silver filled with wine, brown smoking soup-tureen. At table sat man of about forty, merry and open countenance, dandling little child on knees. Close by very young woman nursing another child. Father laughing, child laughing, mother smiling. Stranger paused in reverie before this tender spectacle.**
- **Encountered man of lofty stature, half peasant, half artisan, wearing huge leather apron reached to left shoulder, upheld by girdle with hammer, red handkerchief, powder-horn. Carried head thrown backwards; shirt widely opened displayed bull neck, white and bare. Had thick eyelashes, enormous black whiskers, prominent eyes, lower part of face like snout. With difficulty repassed fence, found himself once more in street, alone, without refuge. Dropped rather than seated himself on stone; exclaimed: "I am not even a dog!"**
- **Walked thus with head drooping. When far from human habitation, raised eyes and gazed searchingly about him. In field before low hill covered with close-cut stubble resembling shaved heads. Horizon perfectly black; not alone obscurity of night but caused by very low-hanging clouds seeming to rest upon hill, mounting and filling whole sky. Moon about to rise; remnant of twilight brightness still floating in zenith; clouds formed whitish arch at summit of sky. Man not sensitive to mysterious aspects of things; nevertheless, something in sky, hill, plain, tree was profoundly desolate. After moment of immobility and reverie turned back abruptly. Nature seemed hostile.**
- **At supper with Bishop: Advanced three paces and approached lamp on table. Stated: "I am a galley-slave; a convict. I come from the galleys." Drew from pocket large sheet of yellow paper, unfolded it—yellow passport to expel him from every place. "I know how to read. I learned in the galleys. There is a school there for those who choose to learn." Described: native of [unspecified], nineteen years in galleys: five years for house-breaking and burglary; fourteen years for attempting to escape on four occasions. "Very dangerous man." Every one has cast him out. Overwhelmed when Bishop accepts him; exclaims: "Really? What! You will keep me? You do not drive me forth? A convict! You call me sir! You do not address me as thou? 'Get out of here, you dog!' is what people always say to me. Oh, what a good woman that was who directed me hither! I am going to sup! A bed with a mattress and sheets, like the rest of the world! It is nineteen years since I have slept in a bed!" Recounts he has spent only twenty-five sous in four days, earned by helping unload wagons at Grasse. Tells Bishop: "We had a chaplain in the galleys. And one day I saw a bishop there. He was the Bishop of Majore at Marseilles—the curé who rules over the other curés. He had a pointed thing, made of gold, on his head; it glittered in bright light of midday. We were all ranged in lines on three sides, with cannons with lighted matches facing us." Responds to Bishop's mercy with anguished recounting of degradation in galleys.**

**Secondary Characters**
- **Maubert Isabeau: Baker on Church Square at Faverolles; victim of Valjean's theft in 1795 when Valjean stole loaf of bread through grated shop front in violent blow**
- Jacquin Labarre: Landlord of Cross of Colbas inn; man of consideration in town due to relationship to Labarre who keeps Three Dauphins inn in Grenoble and served in the Guides; identified Valjean, drove him away
- Fishmonger of Rue de Chaffaut: Encountered Valjean; reported him to Labarre and others
- **Mother Gerbaud: Visited Bishop at supper with little child in arms; received fifteen sous from Baptistine via Bishop's instruction**
- Paulin Musebois: Locksmith; Madame Magloire proposes to summon him
- Marie-Claude: Farmer's wife at Faverolles; lent milk to Valjean's habitually famished siblings
- Jeanne Mathieu (Valjean's mother): Died of milk fever not properly attended to
- Jean Valjean (Valjean's father): Tree-pruner; killed by fall from tree
- Valjean's sister Jeanne: Widow with seven children, boys and girls; brought up Jean Valjean
- **Gaspard Bès: Bandit whose band was destroyed in Ollioules gorges**
- **Lieutenant Cravatte: Bandit who took refuge in mountains near Barcelonette; sent Bishop pontifical vestments stolen from Notre Dame d'Embrun treasury**
- Claude Gaux: Stole loaf of bread (mentioned as parallel case to Valjean's theft); used as example of theft-caused-by-hunger in author's commentary
- **Ignorantin friars: Keepers of school for convicts at Toulon**
- **Peten Haskick: Folk character called "Quiet Peten" (mentioned in passing; context unclear)**
- **Fenelle Lindmere: Mason by trade (mentioned in passing; context unclear)**

## Key Events
- **1795: Valjean at approximately 25-26 years old steals loaf of bread from baker Maubert Isabeau during hard winter when family starving; caught by Isabeau; taken before tribunals for theft and breaking and entering inhabited house at night. Sentenced to five years in galleys.**
- **1795-1814 (19 years): Valjean imprisoned at Toulon in galleys. Clothed in red cassock; assigned number 24,601; lost name and identity. Underwent deep moral meditation on justice, society's responsibility, and his own culpability. Recognized injustice and iniquity of punishment disproportionate to crime. Developed hatred toward society; educated himself (learned reading, writing, arithmetic at age 40) to fortify intelligence and hate. Attempted escape four times, adding fourteen years to sentence. Sister and seven children became unknowable to him after first day of discussion.**
- Early October 1815, afternoon: Jean Valjean arrives in D——; identified by innkeeper Labarre; encounters fishmonger; attempts to find shelter in multiple locations; chased from each; forced to seek refuge outdoors amid hostile nature
- **Early October 1815, evening: Valjean returns to town and proceeds to Bishop's house; at supper confesses his status as discharged convict with yellow passport; Bishop receives him with warmth and dignity; accepts him as guest at table with all silver laid out; explains fruitières of Pontarlier in detail; later sends goat skin to Valjean's bed; makes strange abrupt movement with folded arms and savage gaze, exclaiming in hoarse voice (words unspecified); knelt in private prayer before alcove curtain; walked in garden contemplating mysteries of God. Valjean overwhelmed by acceptance after day of universal rejection.**

## Authorial Commentary
- **Author notes second instance in his studies on penal question and damnation by law encountering theft of loaf of bread as point of departure for disaster: Claude Gaux had stolen loaf; Jean Valjean had stolen loaf. English statistics prove four thefts out of five in London have hunger for immediate cause.**
- **Author poses philosophical question: Does human nature change utterly from top to bottom under oppression? Can man created good by God be rendered wicked by man? Can soul be completely remade by fate, become evil if fate is evil? Can heart become misshapen under disproportionate unhappiness as vertebral column beneath too low vault? Author asserts: Is there not in every human soul, particularly Jean Valjean's, first spark, divine element, incorruptible in this world, immortal in other, which good can develop, fan, ignite, make glow with splendor, which evil can never wholly extinguish?**

## Themes
- Social rejection and systematic exclusion of mysterious stranger
- Hospitality versus suspicion; human dignity denied through appearance and reputation
- Desperation and dehumanization through poverty; stealing bread to feed starving family
- Contrast between domestic happiness and homelessness
- Galley system's dehumanization versus episcopal recognition of human worth
- Injustice and iniquity of legal system: punishment disproportionate to crime; society's culpability for poverty
- Redemptive mercy and Christian charity; transformative power of acceptance and dignity restoration
- Corruption of soul through hate and vengeance developed during unjust imprisonment
- Possibility of redemption and restoration of divine spark despite prolonged dehumanization
- Role of education in human consciousness; danger of enlightenment serving evil ends
